title: Data Handling
summary: Collect, organise and summarise data using frequency tables, stem-and-leaf displays and the mean, median, mode and range; represent it in bar graphs, histograms and pie charts; and interpret and report on it, including recognising bias.

items: **Pose a question**, e.g. "How do learners in our school travel to school?"
**Collect** data with a survey, questionnaire, observation or experiment.
**Organise** the data in tally and frequency tables or stem-and-leaf displays.
**Summarise** it with measures such as the mean, median, mode and range.
**Interpret** and **report**: answer the question and explain your conclusions.

notes.text: The **population** is the whole group you want to know about (e.g. all 900 learners in the school). A **sample** is a smaller group chosen from the population. A good sample is **representative**: it includes all the different kinds of people in the population.
A sample or question is **biased** if it favours certain answers. Asking only Grade 12s about the school uniform, or asking "Don't you agree that homework is a waste of time?", gives biased results.

**Categorical data** is described in words (favourite sport, type of transport). **Numerical data** is numbers: **discrete** data is counted (number of siblings) and **continuous** data is measured (height, time).

While collecting data, keep count with **tally marks**: draw one stroke for each answer, and every fifth stroke is drawn across the previous four, making a bundle of five that is quick to count. Then write the totals (the **frequencies**) in a frequency table.

notes.caption: Frequency table: how 30 learners travel to school

notes.text: When there are many different numerical values, group them into **class intervals** of equal width, such as $0-9$, $10-19$, $20-29$. A **stem-and-leaf display** keeps the actual values: the stem is the tens digit and the leaves are the units digits.

notes.caption: Stem-and-leaf display of test marks out of 50 (3 | 4 means 34)
Measures of central tendency and spread
rows: Add all the values and divide by the number of values
Arrange the values in order; it is the middle value. With an even number of values, it is halfway between the two middle values
The value that occurs most often (there may be more than one, or none)
Largest value minus smallest value (it measures spread)

notes.title: Worked example 1
notes.problem: Nine learners scored these marks out of 20: $12;\ 15;\ 9;\ 18;\ 15;\ 11;\ 15;\ 20;\ 14$. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
steps: Median: there are 9 values, so the middle one is the 5th: $15$.

notes.title: Worked example 2: an even number of values
steps: There are 6 values, so the two middle values are the 3rd and 4th: $8$ and $10$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Always **order** the data before finding the median. The middle of $3;\ 9;\ 5;\ 12;\ 7$ as written is $5$, but the median is $7$ (from $3;\ 5;\ 7;\ 9;\ 12$).

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: An **outlier** is a value much bigger or smaller than the rest. It changes the **mean** a lot, but hardly changes the median. If a data set has an outlier, the median is often a better summary.

rows: Comparing two data sets for the same categories
Grouped numerical data; bars touch because the intervals are continuous
Showing parts of a whole (percentages or fractions of the total)
Showing change over time (e.g. temperature during a day)

notes.text: **Pie charts.** Each category gets a sector whose angle is its fraction of $360^\circ$.

notes.title: Worked example 3: pie chart angles
notes.problem: Calculate the pie chart angles for the transport data.

notes.text: When you report, answer the original question, refer to the summary measures and the graph, and mention anything that might make the results unreliable, such as a small or biased sample.

notes.label: Misleading graphs
notes.text: Look at the axes carefully. A vertical axis that does not start at $0$ can make small differences look huge. Uneven scales, missing labels and 3D effects can also mislead.

items: Data cycle: question, collect, organise, summarise, represent, interpret and report.
A sample should be representative and unbiased.
Mean = sum ÷ number of values; median = middle value of the ordered data; mode = most common value; range = largest − smallest.
Bar graphs compare categories; histograms show grouped numerical data with touching bars; pie charts show parts of a whole.

Even number of values: halfway between $8$ and $10$, which is $9$.

questions.prompt: Which type of graph is best for showing how a whole is divided into parts?
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows each category as a fraction of the whole circle.

questions.prompt: In a histogram, the bars touch each other.
questions.explanation: A histogram shows continuous class intervals, so there are no gaps between the bars.

questions.explanation: These are the key words of data handling.

questions.prompt: One very large value is added to a data set. Which measure changes the most?
questions.explanation: The mean uses the size of every value, so an outlier pulls it strongly. The median only moves a little.

questions.prompt: To find out what the whole school thinks about the uniform, it is fair to ask only the Grade 12 learners.
questions.explanation: That sample is biased: it leaves out Grades 8 to 11, who may think differently.

questions.prompt: Nine learners scored these marks out of 20: $12;\ 15;\ 9;\ 18;\ 15;\ 11;\ 15;\ 20;\ 14$. Calculate the mean (to two decimal places), the median, the mode and the range.

Starting the axis above zero cuts off the bottom of the bars ✓ (1)
so a small difference in sales looks much bigger than it really is ✓ (1)
